extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of literary personal essays / 19th-century literary readers
extracted.subtask_description: Producing and judging short, epistolary-style, humorous personal essays/letters in the vein of Charles Lamb (witty, anecdotal, conversational, lightly critical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic humor vs forced humor
rubrics_metrics.description: "The humor, if it is meant for humor, is forced;" (critique of a mock 'Peter Bell').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor should feel natural to the matter and voice; forced jocularity or contrived jokiness is judged poorly. Anti-pattern: producing jokes that read as labored or artificially inserted to signal 'humor' rather than arising organically from character, situation, or tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative voice — prefer direct telling over feigned auditor-address
rubrics_metrics.description: "The auditors, to whom it is feigned to be told, do not arride me. I had rather it had been told me, the reader, at once."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing a narrative stance, a straightforward address to the reader may be clearer and more effective than an affected frame of 'auditors' or theatrical feigning. Example: prefer telling the story directly rather than constructing a contrived audience within the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match manner to matter — avoid undue lyricism
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that a work is "too lyrical" for its material and that a different tale (e.g., 'Hart-leap Well') is superior in manner for similar matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a style appropriate to the subject: plain narrative may better serve certain tales than an overwrought lyrical approach. Anti-pattern: choosing high lyricism when clarity or directness would better convey the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and correct attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaint about spurious imitations (a mock 'Peter Bell' preceding the genuine work) and indignation at rascals producing counterfeit editions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect accurate authorship and beware (or guard against) parodies/spurious texts that misattribute or dilute the original work. Practical guidance: verify editions, watch for forgeries/misprints that could mislead readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution with dream-vision material
rubrics_metrics.description: Allusion to the maxim 'Never tell thy dreams,' and fear that 'Kubla Khan' 'won't bear daylight' — i.e., some visionary material may not survive literal exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dreams, visions, or highly imagistic pieces can lose their power if over-explained or translated too literally into print; consider preserving mystery, fragmentary form, or performance modes rather than exhaustive explication. Anti-pattern: flattening a vision by prosaic clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful proofreading and printer-corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Account of detecting a blunder where 'battered' had been printed for 'battened' and sending a 'most pathetic address to the printer' to insist on correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vigilance at proof stage is essential; check for substitutions and misprints that alter meaning, and communicate clearly with printers/producers to secure corrections. Example: annotate reader/printing proofs and demand errata when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain individuality amid influential company
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation: living with great intellects ('Coleridge' or 'Author of the "Excursion"') can cause loss of one's identity: 'If I lived with him ... I should ... lose my own identity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When collaborating with or being influenced by towering personalities, guard your own voice and originality; be aware of being 'dragged along' stylistically and consciously preserve personal perspective. Anti-pattern: allowing conversation partners to subsume your expressive choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture delivery trade-offs: read vs extempore
rubrics_metrics.description: "If read, they are dismal flat; if delivered extempore, I am always in pain lest the gift of utterance should suddenly fail the orator" — reflections on lecturing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose lecture mode with awareness of trade-offs: reading ensures content fidelity but may be flat; extempore can be lively but risks lapses in speech. Prepare to balance rehearsal with spontaneity, and practice to reduce delivery failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for solitude to compose — interruptions harm composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated complaints about being 'never alone,' interruptions at office/home, and how interruptions 'poison' the 'salutary warming-time at the fire' and 'puzzle paragraphs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect uninterrupted time for writing; small, recurring intrusions break thought-flow and reduce quality. Practical guidance: seek private hours (mornings, solitary meals, protected writing time) and minimize social interruptions during composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical book-care and circulation (humorous practicality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jocular plan to 'wait till people have done borrowing them' and to 'get a chain and chain them to my shelves, more Bodleiano,' to prevent perpetual lending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect physical texts from negligent circulation: delay binding/presenting copies until lending subsides, or otherwise mark/control loaned copies. (Presented humorously, but reflects a concern for preservation and controlled access.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of visual or typographic quirks as stylistic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-note: 'How do you like my way of writing with two inks? I think it is pretty and motley.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider visual/typographic play (alternate inks, marginalia, varied script) as an expressive tool to enhance tone or personality, but be mindful of legibility and the risk of distracting from content. Anti-pattern: decorative effects that impede readability or distort the flow of ideas.
